content: The term hydrogen ion is recommended by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) as a general designation for all ions derived from hydrogen and its isotopes. Depending on the charge of the ion, two distinct categories can be identified: Cations (positively charged ions) When a hydrogen atom loses its electron, the following cations can be formed: Hydron: This is the general term used to describe the positively charged ion of any hydrogen isotope (H⁺). Proton: Specifically refers to the cation of the most common hydrogen isotope, ¹H⁺. Deuteron: Refers to the cation of the deuterium isotope, ²H⁺ or D⁺. Triton: Refers to the cation of the tritium isotope, ³H⁺ or T⁺. Additionally, when these cations interact with water, they form hydrated ions, which are also referred to as hydrogen ions. These include: Hydronium ion (H₃O⁺): A hydrated form of the hydrogen ion. Zundel cation (H₅O₂⁺): A structure formed during proton transfer processes. Eigen cation (H₉O₄⁺): Another hydrated form of the hydrogen ion. The Zundel and Eigen cations are particularly significant in the context of proton hopping, a phenomenon described by the Grotthuss mechanism, which explains the rapid movement of protons in aqueous solutions. In the context of acids, the term hydrogen ions typically refers to hydrons, as they are central to the behavior of acids in solution. Anions (negatively charged ions) Hydrogen anions are formed when a hydrogen atom gains an additional electron. These include: Hydride: A general term for the negatively charged ion of any hydrogen isotope. Deuteride: Refers to the anion of the deuterium isotope, ²H⁻ or D⁻. Tritide: Refers to the anion of the tritium isotope, ³H⁻ or T⁻. In organic chemistry, a hydrogen atom within a molecule is often referred to simply as a proton, even though it may not always exist in its ionic form. The hydrogen anion has also played a significant role in the field of quantum physics, where its unique properties have been studied extensively.
